title: Can vs. Will: Propensity-Aware Memorization in LLMs
hook: Most memorization tests ask whether you can force a model to spit out training data. This one asks a sharper question: does it leak under ordinary use? The two answers are very different.
key_points: Standard memorization audits measure worst-case extractability — whether a prefix attack can elicit training data.
PropMe instead measures propensity: how much a model leaks under generic, non-adversarial prompts.
Across two fully-open models, prefix attacks elicited strong memorization while propensity scores stayed low.
Continued pre-training on different data lowered both memorization capability and propensity for the original corpus.
content_html: Large language models can reproduce chunks of their training data — but how worried should we be? Barmina and colleagues argue that most memorization evaluations answer the wrong question. They measure whether a model can be forced to regurgitate data (typically by feeding it a prefix of a known passage), not whether it actually does under ordinary, non-adversarial use.
extra_html: Their framework, PropMe, separates the two. It contrasts prefix-based capability attacks with generic and dataset-specific prompts, and proposes a metric transformation that turns existing memorization functions into propensity metrics. A companion tracing pipeline, SimpleTrace (built on infini-gram), deterministically attributes a model's generations back to large training corpora and computes verbatim, near-verbatim, and propensity-transformed scores. Evaluating two fully-open models (Comma and DFM Decoder) on the Common Pile and Dynaword datasets, they find a consistent gap: prefix attacks elicit strong leakage, but propensity stays low — models can reveal training data when directly elicited, yet rarely do in common settings. They also show that continued pre-training on partly different data reduces both capability and propensity. The recommendation: memorization audits should report both worst-case extractability and ordinary-use leakage propensity.

related.title: Deduplicating Training Data Makes LMs Better
related.hook: Training corpora are full of copies — one 61-word sentence shows up 60,000+ times in C4. Strip the duplicates and models memorize far less and evaluate more honestly.

related.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
related.hook: Finding the prompts that make a model misbehave is slow if humans do it by hand. So use another language model to generate those attacks automatically — at scale.

flashcards.prompt: What distinction does the PropMe framework draw that older memorization metrics miss?

choices.text: Capability (can it be forced to leak) vs. propensity (does it leak under ordinary use)
Training-set size vs. model parameter count
Verbatim copying vs. paraphrasing, with no behavioral angle

flashcards.explanation_html: PropMe contrasts prefix-based capability attacks against non-adversarial evaluations — separating whether a model can leak from whether it does in normal use.

flashcards.prompt: What gap did the authors consistently find between capability and propensity?
flashcards.back_html: Prefix attacks elicited substantially stronger memorization signals than generic prompts, while propensity scores stayed low overall — models can reveal training data when pushed but rarely do so otherwise.

flashcards.prompt: How did continued pre-training on partly different data affect memorization?
flashcards.back_html: A model continually pre-trained from another (DFM Decoder from Comma) showed reduced memorization and propensity for the original corpus — memorization can decrease when later training emphasizes different data.
